stories.title: Bridge Investment Group Provides $67M Refi for Value-Add Multifamily Outside Boston
stories.excerpt: Invictus Real Estate Partners has secured $67.2 million to refinance Eliot on Ocean, a 194-unit multifamily property in Revere Beach, Mass., a coastal submarket five miles outside of Boston. Bridge Investment Group Holdings provided the debt, structured as a three-year, floating-rate loan, while a JLL Capital Markets team of Scott Aiese, Tom Sullivan and Alex Staikos arranged the transaction. In a statement, Aiese spoke to the asset’s “irreplaceable location,” particularly because of the property’s transit connectivity, and noted that the deal is a value-add play for the sponsor who aims to capture higher market rents through capital improvements. “Revere Beach represents one of the few remaining value-add opportunities in Boston’s constrained waterfront multifamily market,” said Aiese, who noted that the Revere Beach market has received more than $1 billion in institutional investment since 2015. Located at 660 Ocean Avenue in Revere Beach — a three-mile waterfront corridor that is home to the first public beach in the United States — the seven-story Eliot on Ocean spans 143,252 square feet and opened in 2016. Aside from offering residents direct access to the beach, the apartment complex sits directly on the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority’s Wonderland Blue Line station, offering a trip into Downtown Boston in less than 35 minutes. Invictus Real Estate Partners plans to improve the lobby and shared amenity spaces and improve appliances and finishes throughout the complex, according to JLL. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Bridge Investment Group closes $67.2M refi for 194-unit Eliot on Ocean, Revere Beach, Mass.
Three-year floating-rate structure; sponsor targeting value-add rent growth via capital improvements.
Revere Beach waterfront received $1B+ institutional investment since 2015; supply-constrained Boston submarket.
stories.summary: Bridge Investment Group provided $67.2 million to refinance Eliot on Ocean, a 194-unit multifamily property in Revere Beach, Massachusetts, structured as a three-year floating-rate loan. The sponsor intends to execute a value-add strategy, capturing higher market rents through capital improvements while leveraging the asset's transit connectivity and waterfront location. Revere Beach has attracted over $1 billion in institutional investment since 2015, reflecting its position as one of Boston's few remaining supply-constrained value-add opportunities.
stories.impact: Floating-rate financing on a value-add play signals lenders' confidence in near-term rent growth, but rising SOFR/rates will compress sponsor returns in Boston's tight submarket. Revere Beach's $1B+ inflow suggests institutional capital is chasing limited supply—opportunity window narrowing for ground-up development; existing portfolio acquisitions and selective rehabs will command premium pricing as new supply dries up.

stories.title: Polymarket Bets On a Second Floor at Manhattan’s 78 Crosby Street
stories.excerpt: Predication and betting site Polymarket has doubled its footprint at 78 Crosby Street to 12,700 square feet, adding the fifth floor to the space it already leases on the fourth floor. Polymarket has been headquartered at the Lower Manhattan building since 2023. Its original lease for 6,350 square feet was also extended, with both deals now terminating in a future year that was not disclosed. The tenant was represented by Emilie Goldman of JLL, while property owner Milkystar was represented by Nicholas Judson, Wendy McDonald and Crosby Matthews of Judson CRE. The asking rent for the space was $85 per foot as demand for offices in SoHo has continually increased over the past year. The fourth floor was previously occupied by a satiric iteration of Enron, the Houston-based energy corporation that became the poster child for accounting fraud and filed for bankruptcy in 2001. The company used the floor in 2025 when it launched the fictitious “Egg” as a self-contained nuclear energy source. New York-based Polymarket allows users to bet on the outcome of sports games, the weather, politics and almost anything someone can think of. The 28-year-old founder and CEO, Shayne Coplan, is currently recognized as the world’s youngest self-made billionaire. Since its inception in 2020, Polymarket has raised roughly $2 billion and is now seeking to raise more funds to create a $15 billion valuation. In June, Polymarket processed $10.7 billion in trades on its crypto-based international exchange and $3.3 billion on its regulated U.S. exchange. The platform operates under its parent company, Blockratize.
bullets: Polymarket doubles footprint at 78 Crosby St., Manhattan, adding 5th floor to existing 4th-floor lease.
Asking rent $85/sf; original lease extended; total new space 12,700 sf (prior 6,350 sf).
SoHo office demand surging past year; tenant growth signals tech/fintech expansion in Lower Manhattan.
stories.summary: Prediction and betting platform Polymarket doubled its footprint at 78 Crosby Street in Lower Manhattan to 12,700 square feet by leasing the fifth floor while extending its original fourth-floor lease of 6,350 square feet. The asking rent was $85 per square foot. Both leases extend to an undisclosed future year, with JLL and Judson CRE brokering the transaction. The expansion underscores growing office demand in SoHo over the past year.
stories.impact: SoHo office asking rents of $85/sf reflect tight supply and flight-to-quality among fintech/crypto tenants seeking branded Class-A space; multifamily development in Lower Manhattan and Upper West Side neighborhoods will benefit from this continued tech-sector employment concentration and high-income tenant base, supporting stronger rental demand and pricing power.

stories.title: U.S. Payrolls Unexpectedly Shrink by 23,000 as Unemployment Slips to 4.1%
stories.excerpt: U.S. employers unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, falling far short of the 88,000 gain projected by economic consensus, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.    The drop was compounded by sharp downward revisions to prior months. May payroll additions were revised down by 66,000 to 63,000, while June figures were trimmed by 37,000 to 20,000. Combined, employment across May and June was 103,000 lower than previously reported.  Despite payroll contractions, the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from 4.2% in June, beating the 4.2% consensus estimate. The decline was largely driven by a shrinking labor force, as the participation rate ticked down to 61.4% from 61.5%.  The softening labor data could remove some urgency for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. The figures bolster arguments among policymakers who expect inflation to cool in the second half of the year as housing costs ease and the economic impact of President Trump’s tariffs begins to fade. bullets: U.S. payrolls contracted 23,000 in July; May & June revised down 103,000 combined; unemployment 4.1%.
Labor force participation fell to 61.4% from 61.5%; job losses offset by lower participation.
Softening data reduces Fed urgency to raise rates; inflation and tariff impacts expected to ease.
stories.summary: U.S. employers unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, far below the consensus 88,000 gain projection. Prior months saw sharp downward revisions—May cut by 66,000 and June by 37,000, totaling 103,000 lower employment across the two months. Despite payroll contraction, the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, largely driven by a declining labor force participation rate of 61.4%. The softening labor data and moderating inflation outlook may ease pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise rates.
stories.impact: Unexpectedly weak job growth and falling participation signal slowing demand-side momentum, which could moderate rent growth expectations nationwide and ease competitive pressure on multifamily operators to raise rents aggressively. However, rate-hold or cut expectations improve development financing feasibility (lower SOFR, tighter cap rates) and could unlock stalled value-add and new-construction projects underwritten at higher rate assumptions.

stories.title: Newmark Group CEO Barry Gosin to Step Down at Year’s End
stories.excerpt: Newmark Group, Inc. said Friday that Barry Gosin will step down as CEO at the end of 2026. Gosin has served in this role since 1979. He will continue as chairman of Newmark & Company Real Estate, Inc., Newmark’s operating company, to focus on relevant and impactful topics, as well as to support a seamless transition. “I have spent nearly my entire career at Newmark, working alongside an exceptional team whose dedication, talent and commitment have made the company’s success possible,” said Gosin. “The company is stronger than ever, our strategy is working and the opportunities ahead are substantial, which is why I believe now is the right time to take a step back from day-to-day operations to focus solely on matters that will make a difference to Newmark, and to support the company through this transition.” Added Stephen Merkel, chairman of the board, EVP and chief legal officer of Newmark, “We are delighted that Barry will remain with the company as chairman of the operating company to help the next generation of leadership as they guide Newmark through its next chapter of growth. For nearly five decades, Barry, along with his entire leadership team, have led Newmark through some of its most consequential milestones, including its initial public offering in 2017 and becoming the fastest growing publicly traded commercial real estate firm in the world, increasing annual revenues by over 1,400% since 2011 while expanding to more than 10,000 professionals across approximately 195 locations.” In connection with this announcement, Gosin entered into an amended and restated employment agreement to remain as chairman of Newmark & Co. up to 2029. The board expects to identify a new CEO by year end. The post Newmark Group CEO Barry Gosin to Step Down at Year’s End appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Barry Gosin steps down as Newmark CEO Dec. 31, 2026; held role since 1979.
Gosin transitions to chairman of operating company; successor to be named by year-end.
Newmark operates 10,000 professionals across 195 offices; company positioned 'stronger than ever.'
stories.summary: Barry Gosin will step down as CEO of Newmark Group at the end of 2026 after holding the position since 1979. He will remain as chairman of Newmark & Company Real Estate (the operating company) to support a seamless leadership transition. The board will name a successor by year-end. Gosin noted the company is 'stronger than ever' with substantial growth opportunities ahead.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Newmark leadership transition does not materially affect capital markets, underwriting standards, or financing availability; watch for new CEO's strategic focus (e.g., emphasis on brokerage vs. capital markets services) that could shift broker-provided market intelligence and deal flow to multifamily teams.

At 10,000 professionals over 195 offices, Newmark isn’t the biggest brokerage in the U.S., but that’s intentional. stories.title: TPG AG, Redfearn Capital Acquire Industrial Portfolio for $628M
stories.excerpt: TPG AG U.S. Real Estate and Redfearn Capital have acquired a 5.4 million-square-foot industrial portfolio for $628 million, Commercial Observer can first report. The seller was DRA Advisors, while BDT & MSD Partners provided a $479 million loan in the deal, sources said. The 53-building portfolio, which is roughly 87 percent occupied, includes both logistics and manufacturing properties spread across Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Minnesota, Illinois and Oregon. Shallow-bay industrial assets in high barrier-to-entry markets make up the majority of the portfolio, and TPG AG now plans to add value through capital investment in the properties. The majority of the portfolio assets are in major industrial markets in the Southeast such as Tampa, Atlanta and Charlotte, N.C. In addition to Redfearn, TPG AG purchased the portfolio with two additional operating partners: Atlanta Property Group and Matterhorn Venture Partners. Each will co-manage the portfolio in their respective markets. “This acquisition represents another significant milestone in our investment strategy and reinforces our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the U.S. shallow-bay industrial sector,” Chris Oka, a managing director at TPG AG, said. “We are pleased to continue our long- standing partnerships with best-in-class operating partners Redfearn, Atlanta Property Group and Matterhorn Venture Partners to acquire and operate a portfolio of high-quality assets with strong occupancy, diversified tenancy, and compelling opportunities to create value through active asset management. We look forward to supporting the portfolio’s continued growth.” “We’ve been intentionally building an industrial platform centered on well-located infill assets in markets with long-term demand,” Alex Redfearn, founder, president and CEO of Redfearn Capital, said in a statement. “This transaction accelerates that strategy in a meaningful way. stories.title: The New Role of Transitional Debt in Commercial Real Estate Finance
stories.excerpt: Transitional lending was once viewed as a temporary financing solution. Today, it’s becoming a core strategy for life insurers as banks continue moving out of commercial real estate lending, according to a new report from Nuveen. The report said that lower property valuations, tighter banking regulations and a wave of loan maturities are changing the landscape of commercial real estate financing. As banks reduce their exposure, private credit funds and life insurance companies are stepping in to provide capital to borrowers seeking to bridge the gap between traditional mortgage financing and opportunistic debt. Three Structural Shifts Driving the Market Nuveen identified three long-term trends supporting transitional lending. Banks are changing roles. Following the Great Financial Crisis, banks were the main providers of transitional CRE loans. Today, stricter capital and regulatory requirements have made those loans less attractive to hold on bank balance sheets. Rather than originating loans directly, many banks now provide warehouse financing and back leverage to private credit funds, allowing those lenders to originate loans while limiting the banks’ direct CRE exposure. Property values have reset. The rapid increase in rates disrupted commercial real estate valuations for a time. But Nuveen said that several years of transactions have led to more realistic pricing. The result is a lending environment with lower appraised values, tighter covenant loan structures, and spreads of roughly 25 to 40 basis points above prior-cycle averages. As a result, returns are driven more by the economics of the underlying loan than by financial leverage, creating what the report describes as a more durable risk-return profile. The maturity wall remains. A large share of commercial real estate loans originated during the close-to-zero-interest era are coming due. Bank regulatory constraints reduce balance-sheet appetite; banks shift to warehouse/back-leverage roles.

stories.summary: Transitional debt has evolved from a temporary financing solution into a core strategy for life insurers and private credit funds as banks withdraw from direct commercial real estate lending. Banks face tighter regulatory capital requirements and reduced appetite to hold CRE loans on balance sheets, instead providing warehouse and back-leverage financing to private lenders. Lower property valuations, heightened banking regulations, and a wave of maturing loans are reshaping the CRE financing landscape.
stories.impact: Shift toward non-bank lenders (life insurers, private credit) narrows bank-originated multifamily loan availability and increases borrowing costs and execution risk for standard bridge and construction financing; developers with strong sponsor pedigree or off-market deal sourcing will access private debt, while marginal projects face capital starvation. Opportunity for developers with balance sheets to acquire distressed or value-add assets at wider cap rates as refinance deadlines approach.

stories.title: The Forces Impacting CRE as AI, Energy and Supply Constraints Take Hold
stories.excerpt: When JLL introduced its six forces reshaping global commercial real estate in late 2025, the 2026 outlook was relatively optimistic. The forecast suggested renewed momentum supported by shrinking supply pipelines, economic growth, easing trade concerns, moderating inflation and lower interest rates. Six months later, things have greatly changed. The Middle East conflict, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and continued trade tensions mean global market uncertainties. “For now, we expect somewhat lower growth, higher inflation, and a change of direction in interest rates from what we were anticipating at the start of the year, and that these effects prove temporary and reversible,” JLL said in its recently released “Global Real Estate Outlook Mid-Year, Updated” report. JLL said six structural forces continue to shape international CRE markets. Cost Management as a Strategic Priority Controlling costs was never in doubt. However, energy, commodity and freight disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts elevated cost management from a priority to a primary business driver for corporate leaders. Higher fuel, materials and logistics costs are impacting operating budgets, increasing construction expenses, raising fit-out costs and slowing project timelines. JLL noted that the strategies companies are using to manage costs have not changed. But the urgency behind those efforts has increased. Supply Constraints Create New Opportunities Development pipelines were already shrinking across many property sectors in mature markets. Rising construction costs and uncertainty around project feasibility could limit additional starts. JLL expects well-located secondary assets to benefit from demand spillover, particularly in markets with limited available space. The environment could also create additional opportunities for owners to retrofit and reposition existing properties rather than pursue new construction. The revised forecast expects lower growth, higher inflation, and rising interest rates—reversing early-2026 optimism. Energy, commodity, and freight disruptions have elevated cost management from a priority to a primary business driver, increasing construction expenses, fit-out costs, and project timelines.
stories.impact: Rising construction costs (labor, materials, energy, logistics) directly compress multifamily development margins and extend project delivery timelines; higher inflation and reversing rate expectations increase debt service costs on floating-rate construction and bridge loans. Developers must accelerate entitlements and cost-lock materials, or reset underwriting to assume higher hard costs and longer interest carry—narrowing feasibility on new starts, favoring acquisition of near-complete stabilized assets over ground-up development.

stories.title: Q2: U.S. Industrial Market Moves Toward Balance as Demand Outpaces New Supply
stories.excerpt: The U.S. industrial market showed signs of stabilization in the second quarter of 2026, with demand beginning to outpace new deliveries while developers remained disciplined about adding new supply. Quarterly reports from CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Lee & Associates discuss a sector that is moving beyond the oversupply concerns of the past two years. Vacancy Stabilizes, Demand Improves After steadily increasing for the past several quarters, the national industrial vacancy rate stabilized in Q2. Increased demand for larger warehouse and distribution facilities helped vacancy decline from its late 2024 peak. At the same time, shallow-bay industrial product experienced a modest increase in vacancy, although availability remains relatively tight compared with historical levels. Absorption Outpaces Deliveries For the first time in several quarters, industrial demand outpaced new deliveries, suggesting a market moving closer to equilibrium. Leasing activity also expanded beyond pre-committed space, as tenants absorbed recently completed speculative projects at a faster pace. Third-party logistics providers remained the largest source of industrial leasing activity during the first half of 2026, while manufacturers also contributed to demand growth. Meanwhile, leasing from general retailers and wholesalers declined as more companies continued to outsource their distribution operations to third parties. Developers Maintain Discipline Although the industrial construction pipeline has increased over the past year, development activity has become less frantic and more reasonable, relative to the recent boom cycle. Much of the space currently under construction consists of build-to-suit projects and larger speculative developments of 200,000 square feet or more. Developers have also become more cautious about launching new projects due to elevated interest rates and rising material costs. Outlook: Gradual Growth Ahead Ongoing demand growth and restrain
bullets: U.S. industrial vacancy stabilized Q2 2026; demand outpaced new deliveries for first time in quarters.
Shallow-bay vacancy modest uptick; larger warehouse/distribution facilities drove improved absorption.
Developers disciplined on new supply; third-party logistics (3PL) & manufacturers primary demand drivers.
stories.summary: The U.S. industrial market showed signs of stabilization in Q2 2026, with demand outpacing new deliveries for the first time in several quarters. National industrial vacancy rates stopped rising and began to normalize from late-2024 peaks, though shallow-bay product saw modest vacancy increases. Strong leasing from third-party logistics providers and manufacturers drove absorption of recently completed speculative projects. Developer discipline on new supply suggests a market moving toward equilibrium after two years of oversupply.
stories.impact: Industrial supply rebalancing (supply discipline, rising demand) will support rent growth and cap-rate compression in primary logistics markets; multifamily developers in industrial-adjacent submarkets (Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Inland Empire) benefit from sustained 3PL and manufacturing employment inflows and population growth. Expect logistics-led infill urban multifamily to command premiums as workers cluster near major distribution hubs.

stories.title: Mermaid Inn Restaurateurs Ink 2K SF at 61 West 74th Street for New Eatery
stories.excerpt: Restaurateurs Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith are making a splash on the Upper West Side. The couple and co-founders of New England-style seafood spot Mermaid Inn have selected 61 West 74th Street for their next venture, Commercial Observer has learned. Abrams secured the 2,300-square-foot lease, plus a basement space, at $130 per square foot, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. The site, located between Columbus Avenue and Central Park West and about a block and a half south of Mermaid Inn, previously hosted Patsy’s Pizzeria. The locally beloved pizza joint permanently closed in January, citing the end of its lease and rising costs, West Side Rag reported. Counter Real Estate’s Justin Losh negotiated the new lease on behalf of the landlord, Viking Management. Meridian’s Carson Shahrabani and Noam Aziz represented Abrams. “Danny has an iconic restaurant, the Mermaid Inn, right around the corner, so it’s incredible to see him become the LeBron of the immediate neighborhood,” Shahrabani said in a statement to CO. The Upper West Side’s Mermaid Inn set up shop at 335 Columbus Avenue in 2024, after its longtime home along Amsterdam Avenue shuttered in 2022. Abrams and Smith operate a second Mermaid Inn location in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, as well as Mermaid Oyster Bar locations in Greenwich Village and Times Square. The upcoming restaurant at 61 West 74th Street remains unnamed and its concept undecided, according to Shahrabani. Abrams declined to share additional details on the new lease. Losh and Viking Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Mermaid Inn founders (Abrams, Smith) lease 2,300 sf at 61 W. 74th St., Upper West Side, NYC.
Rent $130/sf; site near Columbus Ave & Central Park West; prior Patsy's Pizzeria tenant.
Rising Upper West Side restaurant costs cited as cause of prior tenant closure in January.
stories.summary: Restaurateurs Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith, founders of the Mermaid Inn, have leased 2,300 square feet at 61 West 74th Street on Manhattan's Upper West Side for a new restaurant concept. The lease was signed at $130 per square foot and includes basement space. The location previously housed Patsy's Pizzeria, which closed in January citing rising costs and end-of-lease terms.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Restaurant leasing activity and rising rents on Upper West Side reflect consumer demand and affluent residential base; sustained restaurant and retail activation signals healthy neighborhood fundamentals supporting adjacent multifamily valuations but does not materially affect supply, demand, capital, or cost in the residential sector.
